rows.title: Kalshi and Polymarket crack down on paid influencers claiming election fraud
rows.standfirst: Influencers are using prediction market odds to sow doubt in vote counting, in some cases in posts paid for by the companies themselves.

rows.title: Why is there a supplement craze if they don’t even work?
rows.standfirst: One reason the $70 billion supplement industry is set to double in the next seven years? Lax regulation.

rows.title: Who should new grads boo more? AI or remote work?
rows.standfirst: Is AI really to blame for young people finding it hard to land first jobs? Is Black unemployment a leading indicator for the rest of the economy? Here’s what the hosts of our Ambies award-winning business podcast think you should take away from the May jobs report.

rows.title: The U.S. adds 172,000 jobs. Many are in restaurants, bars and hotels
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added jobs for the third month in a row in May, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.3%. But wage gains softened and likely failed to keep pace with rising prices.

rows.title: A global World Cup tradition catches fire in the U.S.: Panini sticker collecting
rows.standfirst: Collecting Panini stickers is a World Cup tradition beloved in Europe and Latin America. In the U.S., interest has been building steadily, and this summer, the buzz is bigger than ever.

rows.title: How cellphone carriers prepare for hurricane season with AI, drones and 'cows'
rows.standfirst: Hurricane season is expected to be milder than usual this year. But that's not stopping cell phone companies from pulling out all the stops.

rows.title: What do you actually get when you pay for AI?
rows.standfirst: Just 3% of U.S. households pay for AI for personal use. Sign ups are growing — even though Americans have subscription fatigue.

rows.title: Equinomics, bag fees, and leftover campaign dollars
rows.standfirst: Our listeners have QUESTIONS about the economy. And we have answers. Today on the show, we look at why horse breeding might be slowing down, why airlines charge baggage fees, and where campaign cash actually goes.

rows.title: A former GEO Group executive now runs ICE. The company's government ties run deep
rows.standfirst: David Venturella's appointment as acting ICE director is the latest in a pattern: Many former employees of the private prison company GEO Group end up working at the federal agency, and vice versa.

rows.title: Trump strips job protections from 8,000 federal workers
rows.standfirst: President Trump signed an executive order that puts some 8,000 high-ranking civil servants into a new category of employees who can be fired for any reason.

rows.title: Firings at CBS' '60 Minutes' reflect the fight for media control in the age of Trump
rows.standfirst: The show's new leader says he fired star Scott Pelley for insubordination. Pelley says he was defending the integrity of the show's journalism after three top executives and two reporters were fired.

rows.title: Thieves are targeting the world's copper. This phone company is fighting back
rows.standfirst: The value of copper is rising, and thieves can make money by stripping it from phone poles, streetlights and EV chargers. But those thefts cost the rest of us.

rows.title: There's no business like dough business
rows.standfirst: Have you ever walked around a street, mall, or airport and noticed two or three of the same franchise restaurant within walking distance? Why might one Starbucks or McDonald’s or Wetzel’s Pretzels sometimes be built so close to another? Are they friends or competitors? And how can that possibly be profitable?

rows.title: Can the internet be reclaimed from Big Tech?
rows.standfirst: Why one former senior advisor of the FTC thinks a libertarian myth of the internet has given Big Tech too much power.

rows.title: DOJ is investigating former congressman George Santos for insider trading on Kalshi
rows.standfirst: The disgraced former congressman allegedly bet on whether he would appear at the State of the Union address, prompting federal investigations.

rows.title: Oil prices drop to cheapest level since early days of Middle East conflict
rows.standfirst: Oil prices had already fallen quite dramatically on Thursday and Friday in anticipation of a deal. Trump has posted online that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen after the deal is signed this Friday.

rows.title: Kennedy Center removes Trump's name from the building
rows.standfirst: Workers finished removing President Trump's name from the facade of the Kennedy Center early Saturday, hours after a court-ordered Friday deadline to remove references to Trump from the building.

rows.title: Justice Dept. approves Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
rows.standfirst: The decision paves the way for a proposed $111 billion merger uniting two rival studio giants — Paramount, owner of CBS, and the much larger Warner, which includes HBO and CNN.

rows.title: SpaceX goes public and is now worth trillions. What happens now?
rows.standfirst: SpaceX is now publicly traded, and it’s leaning heavily into space and AI. What does that mean for us humans here on earth?

rows.title: It’s my tree. Why can’t I cut it down?
rows.standfirst: Can the government stop you from cutting down your own tree? In many towns and cities these days, removing a tree now requires a permit. You might have to pay a fee, or promise to plant replacement trees. But sometimes, the city won't let you cut down the tree at all, even a tree in your own backyard.

rows.title: SpaceX IPO makes history as largest ever. Stock gains 19% on first day
rows.standfirst: The initial public offering from the rocket and AI company raised some $75 billion, making the company one of the biggest in the world — and likely making Elon Musk a trillionaire.

rows.title: Door shuts on some immigrant entrepreneurs as U.S. restricts small-business loans
rows.standfirst: For decades, immigrants who are legal permanent residents in the U.S. could get loans through the Small Business Administration, a core pillar of small-business lending. Not anymore.

rows.title: Can smartphones help explain the drop in birth rates?
rows.standfirst: Are smartphones causing people to have fewer children? A provocative new working paper explores the persistent drop in birth rates since the iPhone was introduced nearly two decades ago.

rows.title: Inflation is bad, work from home sad, FIFA World Cup tix NOT a deal to be had
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!). It’s our weekly look at some of the most fascinating economic numbers from the news.

rows.title: SpaceX blasts off with a record-breaking $75 billion IPO
rows.standfirst: Elon Musk's rocket company, recently merged with xAI, raised $75 billion in its initial public stock offering. It's the first of a trio of mega-IPOs from AI companies expected this year.

rows.title: The SpaceX IPO drama explained
rows.standfirst: What the SpaceX IPO, the largest ever, reveals about big tech, the NASDAQ and more big IPOs to come. Sure it will make Elon Musk a trillionaire, but what does this mean for your retirement account?

rows.title: FBI seizing evidence at California plant where chemical tank overheated
rows.standfirst: Federal authorities served a search warrant on Wednesday at a Southern California aerospace facility where a chemical tank overheated last month, forcing 50,000 residents to evacuate because authorities feared an explosion.

rows.title: Inflation tops 4% for the first time in 3 years on spike in gasoline prices
rows.standfirst: Inflation has surged to its highest level in more than three years since the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran, triggering a surge in gasoline prices.

rows.title: Two indicators for lowering the rent
rows.standfirst: One specific type of affordable housing used to be popular in American cities, kept rents low, then nearly vanished. Is it time to reconsider boarding houses and single room occupancy units? If they lowered rents in cities, why did they go away? We have the history.

rows.title: Should we tax AI?
rows.standfirst: Should we tax AI? The AI race has made a lot of people richer … but most of those gains seem to have gone to the wealthy while everyday workers aren't seeing their incomes go up.

rows.title: The real horror of ‘Alien’ and how it explains why we’re not paid enough
rows.standfirst: Maybe the real monster in the Alien franchise isn’t actually the killer alien. Because behind the acid blood and jump scares is an even more insidious horror: a single employer with unchecked power. That employer is named Weyland-Yutani, a mega-corporation that dominates workers across the galaxy.

rows.title: How your phone keeps you scrolling ... even when you want to stop
rows.standfirst: You pick up your phone to do one quick task, and suddenly 20 minutes have flown by without you even noticing. How do apps do that to you? Today on the show, we bring you an episode of Short Wave that explains how your phone is designed specifically to hold your attention.

rows.title: Poll: Most Americans have the summer blues about Trump and the economy
rows.standfirst: A new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds a record low share of Americans approve of President Trump's job performance and his handling of the economy heading into the summer before a key midterm election.

rows.title: Chloe Malle isn’t worried about backlash to her vision for American Vogue
rows.standfirst: Chloe Malle has a new job: steering American Vogue into a new era, and capturing a new generation of readers — ones accustomed to consuming fashion and culture via algorithm rather than the pages of a glossy magazine.

rows.title: Are we in a new era of permanently higher prices?
rows.standfirst: Inflation is at a three-year high. That’s a problem for the Fed. Yet, under the leadership of new chair Kevin Warsh, it opted yesterday not to hike interest rates. So today on the show, who are the winners and who are the losers amidst higher inflation?

rows.title: Here's how much the Iran war cost -- and how its effects will linger
rows.standfirst: More than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched their war on Iran, the costs and aftereffects are felt around the world.

rows.title: With Iran deal, Trump told ships to 'start your engines.' That's not happening yet
rows.standfirst: Iran's control of the Strait of Hormuz inflicted global pain during the months-long conflict with the U.S. and Israel. A tentative deal is in place, but questions remain about the key waterway.

rows.title: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady and hints at rate hike later this year
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rates unchanged Wednesday, and signaled its next move could be a rate increase. It's the first rate decision under the new Fed chairman, Kevin Warsh.

rows.title: Is gambling the reason we have pro sports?
rows.standfirst: To hear author David Bockino tell it, gambling has always been a key ingredient of pro sports in the U.S.—it’s as American as apple pie. Bockino is the author of the new book Over/Under: An Unexpected History of Sports Betting. So what gave rise to this new wave of sports gambling? And what are we risking placing so many bets on games?

rows.title: Can computer hackers get inside your mind?
rows.standfirst: The cyber weapon that might have prevented nuclear war.

rows.title: The war with Iran is making oil changes pricier. And a deal won't solve it
rows.standfirst: The U.S. may be the world's biggest producer of crude oil, but that's not the case for motor oil. The cost of lubricants is soaring, and even a tentative deal to end the war won't solve the problem.

rows.title: More people are juggling work and kids -- and finding they can't give 100% to both
rows.standfirst: A new Pew survey finds many working parents feel they cannot give 100% at either work or home. Benefits like paid sick leave and more affordable childcare could help.

rows.title: Is it a renter's market? It depends on where you live
rows.standfirst: About 40% of rentals on Zillow offer move-in deals, like a month of free rent, thanks to a construction boom that created an apartment surplus in some parts of the United States.

rows.title: Your American Dream is pending review
rows.standfirst: The Trump Administration recently announced changes to how would-be immigrants get green cards. And it’s causing a lot of confusion, fear and even panic. Today on the show, we hear firsthand from people navigating green card uncertainty.

rows.title: Community colleges are kind of underrated
rows.standfirst: Community college is an increasingly popular hack for those who want to change their career. Here’s what you should know about this gateway to economic mobility.

rows.title: Meta considered buying Kalshi before developing its own prediction market app
rows.standfirst: Mark Zuckerberg met with Kalshi's CEO last year about a potential deal, but talks did not move forward. Now Meta is making its own prediction market app.

rows.title: How to eat out without spending a fortune
rows.standfirst: Personal finance and nutrition experts share simple strategies that make it possible to eat out on a budget. One tip? You might have to let go of your fast food delivery habit.

rows.title: What Iran teaches us about why wars start
rows.standfirst: If war is so costly, why do we keep fighting them? We dig into the wars in Iran, Ukraine and Gaza to understand the incentives that lead countries into violence. Today on the show, the five factors that lead to war.

rows.title: Supreme Court cements Trump's power over agencies long considered independent
rows.standfirst: In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court struck down a 91-year-old precedent that has prevented presidents from removing members of independent agencies meant to be a check on his power.

rows.title: Red, white and glowing blue: Trump's push for new reactors reaches the finish line
rows.standfirst: A program initiated by the Trump administration has allowed small companies to rush their testing of several new nuclear reactor designs. Some worry that safety is being compromised.

rows.title: What you should know about your student loans
rows.standfirst: For many of the 43 million Americans with federal student loans, July 1 is a day to mark on the calendar. Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act is introducing stricter borrowing caps and new repayment plans. Today on the show, we talk with NPR’s Education Reporter Cory Turner about the impact.

rows.title: This mindset shift can help you get better at using up your leftovers
rows.standfirst: Don't let your leftovers go to waste. Cookbook authors share clever storage techniques — like an "Eat Me First" box in your fridge — and cooking tricks to help you make the most of your food scraps.

rows.title: We almost had a smartphone in the 90s. Why did it fail?
rows.standfirst: In the early 90’s, a company called General Magic began working on a portable device that would allow people to check email, make phone calls, even play games. It was basically a smartphone. But it never caught on.

rows.title: World Cup fans are missing games after their resale tickets fall through
rows.standfirst: The ordeal has left fans forced to either miss out on a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity or scramble to find new tickets, often costing more and for worse seats.

rows.title: GLP-1 and women, the AI office boom, and RTO: CEO ego?
rows.standfirst: It’s Indicators of the Week (now on YouTube!).

rows.title: AI is pumping out books. Are they any good?
rows.standfirst: Are all these AI books any good? And by good, we mean are people willing to buy them — not whether the prose is singing. We talk to two researchers who’ve got some answers and a travel guide expert on why AI can’t replace first-hand experience.

rows.title: Meta plans to release AI-powered prediction market app, documents show
rows.standfirst: The company is building an app separate from Facebook and Instagram where people can wager on the outcome of real-world events, using "play money."

rows.title: How stock options made him an overnight millionaire
rows.standfirst: In 2019, Juan Hernandez was laid off from SpaceX. Luckily, he still had the opportunity to buy $50K - $60K of the company’s stock and, years later, it’s safe to say the risk was worth it. Today on the show, how stock options built California as a tech hub.

rows.title: Before Kalshi and Polymarket there was the Iowa Electronic Markets
rows.standfirst: Prediction markets aren’t new. Election betting was common until the 1940s, then mysteriously faded away.

rows.title: Congress passes the largest housing affordability bill in decades — and Trump cancels the signing
rows.standfirst: President Trump canceled a signing ceremony for the bill Wednesday, saying Congress must first pass a strict voter ID bill.

frame: Up to15 visible Business-archive cards at four fixed weekly endpoints, restricted to each block; not a full-publication census
